In contrast, females attain sexual maturity at a slightly larger size of 58.3 centimeters [Lp = 58.3 centimeters] total length, a difference that likely reflects the energetic demands of gestation and parturition. This size-based dimorphism in maturation is common among elasmobranchs and is often linked to the need for females to achieve a body cavity spacious enough to accommodate developing embryos and yolk reserves. Comparisons with sympatric batoids indicate that this guitarfish prioritizes offspring quality over quantity, an evolutionary strategy that is effective in stable environments but maladaptive under intense anthropogenic mortality. Such life history traits necessitate cautious fisheries management.

Longevity data for Brazilian guitarfish are limited, but analyses of vertebral banding patterns suggest a maximum lifespan of approximately ten years [am = approximately ten years] when individuals are reared at a water temperature of 26.7 °C [T = 26.7 °C]. This lifespan is intermediate among rhinobatids, reflecting a pace of life that balances relatively slow growth with late reproduction. The combination of late maturity, extended gestation, moderate fecundity, and a decadal reproductive window means that even modest increases in fishing mortality can rapidly erode population resilience.
